questions.question: What is SSH and why is it used?
questions.answer: SSH (Secure Shell) is a cryptographic network protocol used to securely connect to remote Linux servers over an unsecured network. It encrypts all communication between client and server, making it safe to log in, run commands, and transfer files remotely. In DevOps, SSH is used to connect to EC2 instances, configure servers, and deploy code.

questions.question: What is the difference between a private key and a public key in SSH?
questions.answer: The private key is the secret part of the key pair, stored only on your local machine. It is used to prove your identity when connecting. The public key is the matching counterpart placed on the remote server in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys. When you connect, the server checks if your private key matches the public key it has stored — if they match, access is granted. Think of it as: private key = your house key, public key = the lock on the door.

questions.question: Why does Amazon Linux disable password-based SSH authentication by default?
questions.answer: Amazon Linux disables password authentication because passwords are vulnerable to brute-force attacks — automated tools can try millions of password combinations. SSH key-based authentication eliminates this risk because you need the actual private key file to connect, not just a guessable string. Even if someone knows your username and password, they cannot log in without the private key.

questions.question: What are the three Linux permission types and what does each allow?
questions.answer: The three permission types are: Read (r) — allows viewing the contents of a file, or listing files inside a directory. Write (w) — allows modifying a file's content, or creating/deleting files inside a directory. Execute (x) — allows running a file as a program/script, or entering (cd into) a directory.

questions.question: What are the three permission categories in Linux?
questions.answer: Owner (u) — the user who created the file, has the first set of rwx permissions. Group (g) — a group of users who share common access, has the second set. Others (o) — everyone else on the system who is neither the owner nor in the group, has the third set.

questions.question: How do you read the permission string 'drwxr-xr-x'?
questions.answer: Breaking it down: 'd' = directory (not a file). 'rwx' (characters 2-4) = owner has read, write, and execute. 'r-x' (characters 5-7) = group has read and execute, but no write. 'r-x' (characters 8-10) = others have read and execute, but no write. So the owner has full access, and group/others can read and enter the directory but cannot modify its contents.

questions.question: What is chmod and how do you use it?
questions.answer: chmod (change mode) is the command to change file or directory permissions. There are two methods: Symbolic — uses letters like chmod o+rwx filename (adds read, write, execute to others) or chmod u-x filename (removes execute from owner). Numeric/Octal — uses numbers where r=4, w=2, x=1. For example, chmod 755 filename sets owner to rwx(7), group to r-x(5), others to r-x(5).

questions.question: What is chown and when would you use it?
questions.answer: chown (change owner) changes who owns a file or directory. You need sudo/root to use it. Syntax: sudo chown newowner:newgroup filename. For example, sudo chown vikram:devops report.txt changes the owner to vikram and the group to devops. You use it when files are created by the wrong user, or when transferring ownership of files to a new team member.

questions.question: What is umask and how does it affect file creation?
questions.answer: umask is a value that controls default permissions for newly created files and directories. It works by subtracting itself from the maximum defaults (666 for files, 777 for directories). A common umask of 022 results in new files getting 644 (rw-r--r--) and new directories getting 755 (rwxr-xr-x). Run 'umask' in terminal to see your current value.

questions.question: What are SUID, SGID, and the sticky bit?
questions.answer: SUID (Set User ID): When set on an executable, it runs with the file owner's permissions regardless of who launches it. Example: the passwd command runs as root so regular users can update /etc/shadow. SGID (Set Group ID): When set on a directory, new files created inside inherit the directory's group instead of the creator's primary group. Useful for shared team directories. Sticky Bit: When set on a directory, only the file owner, directory owner, or root can delete or rename files inside it — even if others have write permission. /tmp uses this.

questions.question: Walk me through how you would set up SSH key-based access for a new user on an EC2 instance.
questions.answer: (Situation) A new developer needs SSH access to a specific user account on an EC2 instance. (Task) Set up secure, passwordless key-based authentication. (Action) First, generated an SSH key pair on the developer's local machine using ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096 -C their-email. Then, using ssh-copy-id, copied the public key to the user account on the EC2 instance: ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub username@public-ip. This added the public key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the server. Finally, tested the connection with ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_rsa username@public-ip and confirmed passwordless login worked. (Result) The developer could securely connect without password exposure.

questions.question: A developer reports 'Permission denied (publickey)' when trying to SSH into an EC2 instance. How do you troubleshoot?
questions.answer: (Situation) SSH fails with publickey error. (Task) Diagnose and fix within 15 minutes. (Action) Worked through the checklist: 1) Confirmed the instance was running. 2) Verified Security Group allows SSH on port 22. 3) Checked the username — Amazon Linux uses ec2-user, not ubuntu or root. 4) Verified the private key file path is correct in the -i flag. 5) Checked if the key pair file name was duplicated on Windows (case-insensitivity issue). 6) Connected via EC2 Instance Connect as backup, then checked ~/.ssh/authorized_keys contained the correct public key. 7) Fixed the issue by re-running ssh-copy-id. (Result) SSH connection restored in 12 minutes.

questions.question: You notice a script file exists on the server but cannot run it. What steps do you take?
questions.answer: (Situation) A script exists but running it gives 'Permission denied'. (Task) Enable execution. (Action) Ran ls -l script.sh to check current permissions. Saw it was -rw-r--r-- (no execute bit). Ran chmod u+x script.sh or chmod 755 script.sh to add execute permission. Verified with ls -l again to confirm -rwxr-xr-x. (Result) Script ran successfully. Also checked if the script had the correct shebang line (#!/bin/bash) at the top as a secondary issue.

questions.question: A team needs all files created in /shared/project to automatically belong to the 'devteam' group. How do you implement this?
questions.answer: (Situation) Multiple developers create files in /shared/project but each file gets their personal primary group, blocking others. (Task) Ensure all new files automatically get the devteam group. (Action) Set SGID on the directory: chmod g+s /shared/project or chmod 2755 /shared/project. SGID causes files created inside to inherit the directory's group (devteam) rather than the creator's primary group. Also verified with ls -ld /shared/project that the SGID bit was set (shown as 's' in the group execute position). (Result) All new files in the directory automatically belong to devteam, giving all team members access.

questions.question: How would you change permissions on all files in a directory at once?
questions.answer: (Situation) Need to apply consistent permissions to an entire project directory. (Task) Change permissions recursively. (Action) Used chmod with the -R (recursive) flag: chmod -R 755 /path/to/directory. This applies the specified permissions to the directory itself and all files and subdirectories inside it. For ownership, similarly used chown -R username:group /path/to/directory. Verified with ls -lR to check the changes cascaded correctly. (Result) All files and subdirectories had consistent permissions applied in one command.

questions.question: On Windows, your SSH connection fails even though the key pair name is correct. How do you investigate?
questions.answer: (Situation) SSH fails on Windows despite what appears to be the correct key. (Task) Fix the connection issue. (Action) Investigated Windows file system behavior — Windows is case-insensitive, so files named 'key.pem' and 'Key.pem' are treated as duplicates. Checked Downloads folder and found two files with similar names. SSH was confused about which file to use. Solution: created a new key pair with a completely unique name, created a new EC2 instance with that key pair, and confirmed the key name was unique before connecting. Also installed Git Bash to ensure full SSH tool compatibility on Windows. (Result) Connection succeeded with the new unique key pair.

questions.question: You need to enable password-based SSH authentication on an Amazon Linux instance temporarily for a contractor. Walk through the steps.
questions.answer: (Situation) Contractor needs temporary password access and doesn't have SSH keys. (Task) Enable password auth securely. (Action) Connected to the instance via existing key. Opened config file: sudo vim /etc/ssh/sshd_config. Found 'PasswordAuthentication no' and changed to 'PasswordAuthentication yes'. Saved the file. Restarted the SSH service: sudo systemctl restart sshd. Created a temporary user with a strong password: sudo adduser contractor && sudo passwd contractor. Documented the change for rollback. After contractor work was done, reverted the config change and re-disabled password auth. (Result) Contractor got temporary access; security posture was restored afterward.

questions.question: How do you verify that an SSH public key was successfully copied to a user account?
questions.answer: (Situation) After running ssh-copy-id, need to confirm the key is in place. (Task) Verify authorized_keys content. (Action) Switched to the target user account (su - vikram) or used sudo. Navigated to ~/.ssh/ with ls -la to confirm the .ssh directory exists. Opened the authorized_keys file: cat ~/.ssh/authorized_keys. Confirmed the public key content matches what's in the local ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub file. Also checked that the .ssh directory has chmod 700 and authorized_keys has chmod 600 — SSH requires these exact permissions. (Result) Key confirmed present and permissions verified.

questions.question: A critical file on a production server has chmod 777. Why is this a security problem and how do you fix it?
questions.answer: (Situation) Audit reveals a production config file with 777 permissions. (Task) Assess risk and remediate. (Action) chmod 777 means every user on the system (including potentially malicious processes) can read, modify, and execute the file. For a config file, this is especially dangerous — attackers could inject malicious configuration or steal credentials. Fix: determined the correct owner and group. Set appropriate permissions: sudo chmod 640 /path/to/config (owner read+write, group read, others nothing). Used sudo chown appuser:appgroup /path/to/config to ensure correct ownership. Reviewed audit logs to check if the file had been modified. (Result) File secured with least-privilege permissions.

questions.question: How would you restrict directory access so only the owner can enter it, even though the directory is publicly readable?
questions.answer: (Situation) A directory must be visible in listings but only accessible to its owner. (Task) Set appropriate permissions. (Action) Used chmod 700 /path/to/dir — this gives the owner full rwx access (read to list contents, write to create/delete, execute to enter), while group and others get no permissions at all. Result shown in ls -l: drwx------. Tested by switching users and confirming 'Permission denied' on cd attempts. Note: even sudo users will be blocked unless they use 'su -' to switch to the owner or use sudo explicitly with the full path. (Result) Directory secured — only owner can enter.

questions.question: In a microservices architecture on AWS, why would you use SSH key-based authentication over password authentication for EC2-to-EC2 communication?
questions.answer: SSH key-based authentication is preferred for automated, service-to-service communication for several reasons: No password storage risk — passwords stored in config files or environment variables are a major attack surface. Keys can be scoped to specific users — a deployment script can have its own key pair with access only to what it needs. Audit trail — key-based logins are easier to audit and revoke. AWS Systems Manager Session Manager or IAM role-based access is preferred over direct SSH for service-to-service, but when SSH is used, keys are far safer than passwords. Password rotation is error-prone at scale; key rotation is scripted via AWS Secrets Manager or similar tools.

questions.question: How would you design a secure file permission strategy for a multi-user web application server on EC2?
questions.answer: For a multi-user web application: Web files (/var/www/html) owned by a 'webapp' service user, group 'webdev' for developers. Directories: chmod 755 (owner full, others read+traverse). Config files with secrets: chmod 640, owned by webapp:webdev. Log files: chmod 644 or 640. No files should be 777 in production. Use SGID on shared directories so new files inherit the 'webdev' group. Use the sticky bit on upload directories to prevent users from deleting each other's uploads. Private keys and .env files: chmod 600. Implement a umask of 027 for the web service user (new files get 640, directories get 750). Regular permission audits with 'find / -perm -o+w -type f' to find world-writable files.

questions.question: Explain the security implications of the SUID bit and how it can be exploited. How does AWS recommend protecting against SUID abuse?
questions.answer: SUID allows a program to run with the file owner's privileges (often root). This is intentional for programs like passwd and ping that need elevated access briefly. Security risk: if an SUID binary has a vulnerability (buffer overflow, injection), attackers can exploit it to gain root access — this is called privilege escalation. Finding SUID binaries: 'find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null'. AWS security best practices recommend: removing unnecessary SUID bits from binaries not needed for your application, using AWS Inspector to audit SUID files, applying OS patches promptly since SUID exploits often target known CVEs, and running workloads in containers where the file system is immutable (read-only root filesystem), eliminating SUID risks entirely.

questions.question: How do SSH key permissions interact with IAM roles in AWS, and when would you use one over the other?
questions.answer: SSH key pairs and IAM roles serve different purposes in AWS: SSH key pairs are used for OS-level access — connecting to the EC2 instance's Linux shell. IAM roles are used for AWS API access — allowing the EC2 instance to call AWS services like S3, DynamoDB, etc. When to use SSH keys: Initial instance setup, debugging, direct file management. When to use IAM roles: Application code accessing AWS services, cross-service communication, avoiding hardcoded credentials. Best practice (AWS Well-Architected): minimize direct SSH access in production — use AWS Systems Manager Session Manager for shell access (requires IAM permissions, logs everything, no open port 22). Use IAM roles attached to EC2 instances for application permissions, and SSH keys only for emergency/admin access with strict Security Group rules.

questions.question: What is the security risk of running 'chmod -R 777 /' and how would you recover a Linux system if this happened accidentally?
questions.answer: chmod -R 777 / is catastrophic: every user gets full read/write/execute on all files including /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow (password hashes exposed), /etc/sudoers (privilege escalation possible), SSH keys, and all application secrets. Recovery process: 1) Immediately take a snapshot of the instance before making changes. 2) On AWS — stop the instance, detach the root EBS volume, attach to a healthy rescue instance. 3) Mount the affected volume and restore permissions using a reference file (from a healthy identical instance or from package manager checksums: 'rpm -Va' on Amazon Linux lists files with wrong permissions). 4) Restore critical files first: /etc/shadow (chmod 000), /etc/sudoers (chmod 440), /etc/ssh/sshd_config (chmod 600), /root/.ssh (chmod 700), key system binaries (chmod 755). 5) Full recovery is extremely time-consuming — the practical recommendation is to terminate the instance and replace with a clean AMI.
